candidates.title: Neewer’s 100W ring light can light your face as well as charge up to 3 phones
candidates.full_text:
Pause any beauty tutorial on YouTube and zoom in on the creator’s eyes, and you’ll probably spot two tiny white donuts staring back at you. That’s the signature catchlight of a ring light, a look fashion photographers chased with ring flashes for decades before TikTok made it the default face of the internet. Once you notice the donuts, you’ll see them everywhere, so apologies in advance for ruining every livestream you watch from now on. NEEWER’s two new ring lights take different approaches to creating that look. The RH100B is a 19-inch, 100W studio ring with room for three phones, while the RB18B is an 18-inch edge-lit ring with a built-in battery.

The RH100B is the brighter of the pair, rated at 8,030 lux at about 1.6 feet (0.5m) at a daylight-balanced 5600K, with a Silent Mode for anyone recording voice nearby. Its three phone holders let you shoot a vertical TikTok, a horizontal YouTube video, and a tight close-up at once. The RB18B is designed for softer light, directing its LEDs through a diffusion panel from the edges to reduce hotspots. NEEWER rates its battery life at about 70 minutes at full power, giving you a little over an hour to finish a glam look without an outlet. Both offer a CRI rating of 97+ and a color temperature range of 2900K to 7000K.

Those 768 LEDs run at up to 100W in Smart Mode, with output rated at 8,160 lux at 1.6 feet (0.5m) at 4400K. All that power makes heat, so NEEWER added active cooling with two fan modes. Silent Mode drops output to 80W to reduce fan noise, a useful trade when a podcast mic sits a foot from the ring. Color temperature adjusts in 100K steps and brightness in 1% increments, giving you finer control when matching a warm bedroom lamp or a cool window. Twelve FX scenes, including candlelight, offer additional lighting effects.

Three phone holders and three cold shoes let you mount phones for a vertical TikTok feed, a horizontal YouTube feed, and product close-ups on one stand, with room for accessories. Live sellers will get it instantly, since juggling platforms is half the job. USB-C and USB-A ports, each rated at 5V/2A, can supply power to connected phones, while an 8V DC output can power a compatible camera through a dummy battery, a battery-shaped power adapter. Controls are available through a touch panel with an OLED readout, a 2.4G remote, or the NEEWER app. Compared with NEEWER’s RL-18, a 55W ring with 240 LEDs, fixed 5600K output, and a single knob, the RH100B offers considerably more control over light and connected devices.

Rather than aiming its LEDs straight at your face through a frosted cover, the RB18B tucks its 288 LEDs along the edges and directs them sideways into a diffusion panel. It’s the same general approach used in an edge-lit TV or laptop screen: spread the light before it reaches the viewer. Here, the design aims for a more evenly illuminated ring with fewer hotspots, a welcome consideration during a long makeup session. It runs at 45W and is rated at 3,800 lux at 1.6 feet (0.5m). Its CRI 97+ and TLCI 98+ ratings, the latter a measure of color rendering for television cameras, indicate an emphasis on accurate color reproduction.

Inside sits a 14.4V, 3500mAh battery, roughly 50Wh, rated for about 70 minutes at full power or up to two hours in ECO mode. That makes it an option for a makeup session in a hotel suite or a demo at a pop-up booth with no outlet in sight. NEEWER says a 100W USB-C PD charger refills it in about 100 minutes with the light off, and the light can also operate while plugged in. A 2.4G remote adjusts color and brightness from up to 49 feet (15m) away, while a separate wireless shutter remote triggers your phone camera, letting solo creators make adjustments and take photos from the chair. The stand reaches 69.7 inches (177cm), and the kit packs into a carrying case.

The RH100B sells for $209.99 on NEEWER’s US site, and you’ll also find it at Amazon, B&H, Adorama, and Best Buy. The RB18B lists at $299.99, a $90 premium that buys you a battery, softer edge-lit output, and freedom from the wall. Both come as complete kits with a stand, remotes, and a carrying bag. Your timing is pretty great, too, since NEEWER’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale runs November 19

candidates.title: A 12-inch aluminum cube that unfolds into a whole camp kitchen, with a sink and a grill to match
candidates.full_text:
Algorithm Overland’s Kitchen Cube packs a full camp kitchen into one 12-inch aluminum cube that opens into a serving station. Plates, cups, cutlery and spices for two to five people ride inside, each piece held in its own place.

Camp kitchens sprawl across bins, bags and tailgates on most trips, with the forks in one place, the plates buried somewhere else entirely, and the cups turning up only after the first meal has already been served without them. The spice jar usually rolls under a seat somewhere between the trailhead and the first night out under open sky at camp.

The Amazon route is a different animal. The Mazatzal storage box folds out into a table top and works as a camp kitchen organizer for overlanding and tailgating, at a fraction of the Cube money. It’s plastic and metal, not machined aluminum, and it doesn’t carry a fitted place-setting kit inside.

Packed, the Kitchen Cube measures 12 by 12 by 12 inches. It’s aircraft-grade aluminum. The design carries a U.S. patent pending, the Cubes are made in the USA, and this one ships from New Jersey.

Each person gets a knife, fork, spoon and teaspoon. Each person also gets one stainless steel plate, one thermal cup for hot drinks and one stainless steel tumbler for cold drinks at the table. Sets run for 2, 3, 4 or 5 people, so a couple and a family of five order the same cube in different depths of kit.

An off-grid spice kit rides inside too, holding 3 tubes plus salt, pepper and 3 spices in their own fitted slots. That sounds minor until the second night of plain camp food reminds you why seasoning travels in the first place on any longer route.

The packed cube also changes how the rig loads before a trip ever starts, because one square case stacks and straps down far more cleanly than a soft bag full of loose kitchen gear. A tailgate, a truck bed and a camper floor all take the same footprint, and the kit arrives at camp in the same shape it left home in the morning. That consistency is the quiet selling point here for overland travel.

Price: From $786 Where to buy: Buy at Algorithm Overland

The Sink Cube packs into 13.5 inches and weighs 20 lb. It opens into a washing station with a basin, a pump faucet and a 1.5-gallon water tank feeding that faucet, plus a roll-out stainless drain rack for drying dishes right there. A wood cutting board, a spice rack and a soap dispenser ride inside too.

Cleanup stops being a bin problem once the sink is set up at camp, because washing happens where the meal happened instead of hours later. Dirty plates get washed on site instead of riding home crusted, and the drain rack also works as a basket for fruit and vegetables over the sink during prep work at the table.

The Grill Cube is heavier. At 35 lb in the same 13.5-inch packed size, it carries a charcoal grill with a grate and a flat griddle surface. A portable gas stove rides inside too, plus a cutting board, spatula and spice rack. Charcoal and gas fuel aren’t included in that price, so both belong in the trip budget before the first outing with this cube. The maker flags outdoor use only for this one, with carbon monoxide and fire hazard warnings on the cooking gear, and those warnings sit right on the product page for buyers to read before they order.

Price: From $1,250 Where to buy: Buy at Algorithm Overland

Price: From $1,300 Where to buy: Buy at Algorithm Overland

Trail-Ready starts at $786 for a 2-person set in the standard Brushed Aluminum finish described above. Pro Overlander starts at $876. That $90 step adds a portable camping stove, a pot and pan set, a steel turner and a compact grater set. Those pieces sit on top of everything Trail-Ready already carries inside the cube for cooking at camp. Bring your own stove, and Trail-Ready is enough.

Brushed Aluminum is the standard finish across the system, and Black or Olive adds $50 on every Cube you order. Camel is coming later on the Kitchen Cube only, so there’s no Camel pre-order path today for buyers who’ve set their hearts on that particular finish.

Here’s the tradeoff, plainly, and it runs in both directions at once for anyone pricing this system against simpler camp gear. You get a fitted, machined aluminum kitchen that packs into cubes and sets up the same way every night at camp. The cost runs the other way too, though, because you pay fitted-kitchen money for that order and you wait on a pre-order window before anything ships.

candidates.title: This Handmade Bluetooth Speaker Hides a Deadpan Face Behind its Grille
candidates.full_text:
Touch the body of the BLASÉ 01 and two narrow eyes slowly appear behind its fabric grille. They’re the sort of eyes that make you wonder if the speaker approves of your taste in music, though it doesn’t seem particularly invested either way. Hand-built in Vilnius, Lithuania, this Bluetooth loudspeaker is getting a first run of 20, each with that same sleepy stare.

With its eyes dark, there’s something of a table lamp about it. A broad, matte olive head sits neatly on a tapered pedestal finished in oak veneer. A loop of vegetable-tanned leather curves behind the head, and the pale Kvadrat grille looks more like upholstery than a panel of electronics. A little notch along the lower rim supplies the hint of a frown.

The cloth does some of the acting. It keeps the LEDs out of sight when they’re dark and softens their outlines when they light up, so the face appears without a screen taking over the front. In Blasé mode, that first slow look gives way to a subdued glow. It could keep you company through dinner without asking you to look up.

Tap the body again and Party mode lets the eyes respond to the rhythm. A guest might catch a flash during a song and turn back toward the speaker to see if it happens again. The light is confined to two little marks near the top of the grille. It can follow the beat without ever looking all that excited about joining in.

A third tap puts it in Off mode, which cuts the lights and switches off the microphone without interrupting playback. The mic drives the eyes, and it doesn’t record or send any audio. There’s no voice assistant to summon, either. You can change the speaker’s mood without reaching for a phone or opening an app.

That odd shape has acoustic logic behind it. The head holds the full-range drivers, while the flared leg houses a woofer and two passive radiators. So the piece that looks like a stand is doing part of the work when the bass comes in. The tuning is designed to be midbass-forward, without promising the sort of low end you’d expect from a subwoofer.

It stands about 11.8 inches tall and weighs roughly nine pounds, so that leather loop shouldn’t fool you into thinking this is a picnic speaker. Bluetooth 5.0 handles playback, but there’s no battery. A USB-C cable comes in the box without the required 65W adapter, which makes an outlet and a spare charger part of the plan when you pick a spot.

The first batch of BLASÉ 01 is listed at €720 (about $791), with European Union shipping planned first and no public ship date. That’s a fair amount to spend on a speaker whose biggest party trick is an unimpressed stare, though being handmade and hand-tuned does carry some of that price tag. Still, the cheekiest thing about those eyes is that they can vanish completely, leaving an object you might have put on the sideboard anyway.
